summary: Defines a MIB module for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, networks and services. It gives SNMP tools standard objects for monitoring and configuring ATM equipment. It obsoletes RFC 1695.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the standard SNMP objects for managing ATM networks. A management tool reads and writes these named counters and settings to configure ATM interfaces, set up virtual connections and read error statistics, no matter which vendor made the equipment.

subtitle: The standard SNMP objects for managing ATM interfaces, virtual connections and AAL5 on hosts and switches.

tldr.problem: ATM equipment has many small counters and settings, and without a shared vocabulary each vendor's management tools work only on that vendor's boxes.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module: named objects, arranged in tables, that a network manager reads and writes over SNMP to configure and monitor ATM interfaces, virtual path and virtual channel links, cross-connects and AAL5 connections.
tldr.outcome: A manager can set up a virtual path or channel link step by step, check the negotiated parameters of a link, and read per-connection AAL5 error counters. The document replaced RFC 1695 in 1999.

today: RFC 2515 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 1695 in 1999 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The textual conventions and object identities it uses were split out into a separate module in RFC 2514.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The document defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. In particular, it describes objects used for managing ATM-based interfaces, devices, networks and services.

ATM is Asynchronous Transfer Mode, the cell-switching technology built for constant-delay connections. The MIB covers the local configuration of ATM interfaces, the virtual path and virtual channel links that carry traffic over them, the cross-connects that join links together inside a switch, and the AAL5 layer that carries data such as IP over ATM. The purpose of the memo is primarily to manage ATM permanent virtual connections; switched connections are also represented, though full management of them needs more than this memo provides.

The memo replaces RFC 1695. The changes relative to that earlier version are summarised in the revision clause of the MIB module itself, and the module complies with SMIv2.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives network managers a shared set of names for the things they need to control and measure on ATM equipment. Anything that speaks SNMP can then read an ATM switch the same way it reads a router.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The SNMP management framework has five major components: an overall architecture; the mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events, called the Structure of Management Information (SMI), whose first version is SMIv1 and whose second is SMIv2; the message protocols for transferring management information, SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3; the protocol operations for accessing that information, with PDU formats defined in RFC 1905; and a set of fundamental applications, together with view-based access control.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the MIB, and objects in that store are defined using the mechanisms of the SMI. This memo specifies a MIB module that complies with SMIv2. A module conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the translated module is semantically equivalent except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, for instance the use of Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the protocol managers use to ask devices what they are and to tell them what to do. The MIB is the shared catalogue of things they can ask about. This document adds the ATM part of that catalogue.

sections.title: The ATM Terms the Objects Use
sections.content:
ATM virtual connections come in two kinds. A Virtual Channel Connection (VCC) is a chain of virtual channel links, each one called a Virtual Channel Link (VCL), joined at each switch. A Virtual Path Connection (VPC) works the same way with virtual path links (VPLs). The VCI and VPI fields in the ATM cell header tie each cell to a particular link on a physical link, and switches route cells between links by cross-connecting them according to those values. A VCC is bidirectional by definition, although the traffic parameters of the two directions can be symmetric or asymmetric; a one-way flow is expressed by assigning zero bandwidth in one direction, and even that direction needs bandwidth for operations traffic.

A Permanent Virtual Connection is a provisioned VCC or VPC. A Switched Virtual Connection is set up in real time by call setup signalling. A Soft PVC is a connection in which some portions are switched and others permanent. Any of them can be point-to-point, point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint.

Traffic is policed at resource access points to keep it inside the negotiated parameters, using Usage Parameter Control at a user-network interface, and shaped on the outgoing side to smooth the inter-arrival time of cells. During congestion, cells with CLP=0 have priority over cells with CLP=1, so CLP=1 cells are dropped first. The earlier QoS Class object is deprecated and replaced by a service category.
sections.plainLanguage: A virtual connection is a path through the network built out of short labelled pieces, one per switch. The names in this section are the ones the managed objects use, so it is worth knowing that a virtual path carries virtual channels and a cross-connect joins two of them inside a switch.

sections.title: The Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The managed ATM objects are arranged into six groups: the ATM interface configuration table; the ATM interface DS3 PLCP and TC sublayer tables, which carry performance statistics for the sublayers that carry ATM cells over DS3 and SONET paths; the ATM traffic parameter table; the ATM interface virtual link configuration tables; the ATM virtual path and virtual channel cross-connect tables; and the AAL5 connection performance statistics table. Objects for activating and deactivating operations cell flows, and traps that report virtual connection or link failures, are outside the scope of the memo.

The cross-connect tables work differently depending on the connection type. For a permanent virtual connection, the cross-connect between two virtual paths is held in the ATM VP cross-connect table, indexed by the identifiers of the two paths, and the same holds for channels in the VC cross-connect table. For a switched or soft connection those cross-connects live in the separate ATM2-MIB instead.

The traffic parameter table holds rows of self-consistent ATM traffic parameters, each with a traffic descriptor type, up to five numeric parameters, a service category and a row status. The virtual link tables point at those rows from their receive and transmit traffic descriptor index objects, so a manager selects the parameters it wants rather than repeating them per link. A row is deleted by setting its row status to destroy, and the agent refuses the request while the row is still in use by a virtual link.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are grouped into tables, one per kind of thing: interfaces, traffic parameters, links, the joins between links, and AAL5 connections. Traffic parameters live in their own table so several links can share the same settings.

sections.title: Setting Up a Virtual Link
sections.content:
A virtual path link is created with a negotiated establishment. The management application creates an entry in the VPL table by setting the row status to createAndWait, which fails if the chosen VPI value is unavailable or already in use. The manager then selects an existing row in the traffic descriptor table, which chooses the traffic parameters and the service category for both directions of the link, and creates a new row there if none fits. It points the receive and transmit traffic descriptor index objects at the chosen rows, and the agent checks resource availability and may refuse. If the transmit and receive service categories disagree, the agent should refuse. The manager then sets the row status to active, and the agent reserves the resources needed for the requested parameters and service category. Finally, if the link terminates a virtual path in the host or switch, the manager sets the administrative status to up; otherwise the cross-connect tables are used to join it to another path.

The same work can be done in one step by setting the row status to createAndGo with all the parameter values in a single request, at the cost of the step-by-step error checking. A link is released by setting its row status to destroy, and the agent may then release the associated resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Creating a link is a small conversation with the agent. Ask for a row, say which traffic parameters you want, then switch it on. Each step can fail with a clear reason, which is why the document also explains how to do it in one shot when you do not need the explanations.

sections.title: Applying MIB II to ATM
sections.content:
For the purposes of the sysServices object in the System Group of MIB II, ATM is a data link layer protocol, so sysServices has the value 2 for ATM switches and networks. The Interfaces Group of MIB II defines generic objects for managing interfaces, and this memo supplies the media-specific extensions for ATM interfaces. Each sub-layer below the internetwork layer of an interface counts as an interface, so the ATM cell layer appears as an entry in the interfaces table, concerned with the cell layer as a whole rather than with individual virtual connections.

That entry uses the value 37 for ifType. The physical address is the ATM address at the protocol sublayer, used as the Called Party Address Information Element of a signalling message for a connection that terminates at the interface or whose address would be rewritten before forwarding. The octet counters count cells multiplied by 53. Incoming errors count cells dropped because of uncorrectable header errors, and unknown protocol discards count cells discarded during cell header validation, including cells with unrecognised VPI or VCI values.

The AAL5 layer has its own entry in the interfaces table, with the value 49 for ifType, the largest processable PDU size in the MTU field, and counters for CRC-32 errors, segmentation and reassembly time-outs and oversized service data units. A proprietary internal virtual interface, used inside a switch to reach the AAL5 process, takes the value 53.
sections.plainLanguage: The generic interface table gets a new flavour for ATM. Each ATM port, each AAL5 connection endpoint and each internal interface is one row, with the counts expressed in cells rather than bytes.

sections.title: AAL5 Entities and Their Statistics
sections.content:
AAL5 is the adaptation layer that lets data such as IP ride over ATM cells. In a switch, AAL5 is managed in two ways: as an internal resource of the switch, and per virtual connection. AAL5 in a switch is managed only for the virtual connections that carry AAL5 and terminate at the AAL5 entity in that switch. The switching fabric sends those virtual channels to the virtual channels of a proprietary internal interface associated with the AAL5 process, so the resource is modelled with the interfaces table through that internal interface, and the per-connection performance is modelled with an additional AAL5 connection table in the ATM MIB.

In a host, the AAL5 sublayer sits directly on the ATM sublayer and is managed with the interfaces table. The AAL5 connection table gives performance information for each AAL5 virtual connection terminated at an AAL5 entity in a switch or a host. It is indexed by the interface, the virtual path identifier and the virtual channel identifier, and holds counters for CRC errors, segmentation and reassembly time-outs and oversized service data units.
sections.plainLanguage: AAL5 is where ordinary data such as IP is packed into ATM cells. The MIB counts errors on each AAL5 connection separately, so a manager can see which connection is losing data and why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of objects in this MIB have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Supporting SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The objects in this MIB contain sensitive information, because collectively they allow tracing and influencing virtual connections in ATM switches and networks and reveal their traffic characteristics. It is therefore important to control even read access, and possibly to encrypt the values of these objects when sending them over the network with SNMP. Not all versions of SNMP provide the features needed for such a secure environment. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even where the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on that network may read or change the objects.

The document recommends that implementers use the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. It is then the responsibility of the customer or user to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to this MIB is configured to give access only to principals that have legitimate rights to read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: These objects can change the shape of the network, so anyone who can write them can reroute traffic. The document recommends SNMPv3 with its user-based and view-based access control, and says that even read access needs restricting.
